transcript.text: Good morning. Today's lecture is about traditional crafts and why they matter for cultural heritage. I'll look at three examples, and then discuss the threats these crafts face and some possible solutions.
transcript.speaker: DR AMIN

transcript.text: I should begin with a definition. A craft is a skill of making objects by hand, usually with simple tools, and passed from one generation to the next. It is different from industrial production, where machines make thousands of identical items.
transcript.speaker: DR AMIN

transcript.text: Let me begin with the shyrdak, a felt carpet made in Kyrgyzstan. Craftswomen make it from wool, which is washed, dyed and pressed together, and then decorated with patterns that symbolise animals and mountains.
transcript.speaker: DR AMIN

transcript.text: A good shyrdak can take several weeks to complete, and the pattern is often planned in the head of the maker rather than drawn on paper. Families sometimes keep their best carpets for weddings and other important occasions.
transcript.speaker: DR AMIN

transcript.text: Moving to Japan, we find raku pottery, which is known for its dramatic firing process. The pot is heated in the kiln for only about fifteen minutes, then removed while still glowing and cooled rapidly, which creates the cracks in the glaze.
transcript.speaker: DR AMIN

transcript.text: Finally, kente cloth from Ghana. Traditionally, the weavers used silk, though today cotton is more common because it's cheaper. Each pattern has a meaning, and some designs were once reserved for royalty.
transcript.speaker: DR AMIN

transcript.text: These examples come from very different parts of the world, but they have something in common: each of them carries meanings and stories as well as being a useful or beautiful object. When the craft disappears, those meanings can disappear with it.
transcript.speaker: DR AMIN

transcript.text: Why do these crafts matter? UNESCO has a list of what it calls intangible cultural heritage, which includes skills and traditions rather than buildings or monuments.
transcript.speaker: DR AMIN

transcript.text: One of the biggest threats is cheap factory-made copies, often sold to tourists. These are produced in huge numbers and sold at a fraction of the price, which makes it hard for real craftspeople to earn a living.
transcript.speaker: DR AMIN

transcript.text: Tourists are not to blame, of course. Most of them would prefer to buy something authentic, but they often cannot tell the difference between a handmade piece and a good copy, especially when they are in a hurry and the sellers use similar words.
transcript.speaker: DR AMIN

transcript.text: Another threat is that young people are leaving villages, so there is nobody to learn the skills. In some regions, the average age of master weavers is over sixty.
transcript.speaker: DR AMIN

transcript.text: Some communities have found solutions. Cooperatives allow craftspeople to sell directly to customers online, cutting out the middlemen who take a large share of the profits.
transcript.speaker: DR AMIN

transcript.text: Technology can help in other ways, too. Some workshops now use video to record the process, so that young people can see exactly how a master craftsperson works, even if they live far away from the village.
transcript.speaker: DR AMIN

transcript.text: Schools can help too. In parts of Kyrgyzstan, children now take a weekly workshop to learn felt making from older relatives, which keeps the tradition alive for the next generation.
transcript.speaker: DR AMIN

transcript.text: To conclude, protecting crafts is not about preserving the past in a museum, but about keeping living skills useful. Thank you for listening.
transcript.speaker: DR AMIN
